description: We’re a small team with backgrounds in software/data science and mechanical engineering, excited to learn and build together for the Field Shift challenge. Between coding, data analysis, and physical systems thinking, we want to turn NASA Earth science data into something genuinely useful for farmers

High-level project summary

We talked to a farmer near Boise, Idaho, and the first thing they worried about was water. In the Treasure Valley, next summer's irrigation water depends on this winter's mountain snow, and a dry year can turn a profitable crop into a loss.

Patato is a web app that helps farmers pick next season's crop with that in mind. A farmer draws their field on a map and answers a few simple questions. Patato then pulls NASA weather, satellite water use, snowpack and soil data for that exact field, and ranks crop options by how well they grow there, how they hold up in a dry year, rough income compared with what they grow now, and soil health.

It doesn't replace the farmer's judgment. It puts 25 years of NASA data behind a decision they already have to make every winter.

Detailed project description

What it does

  1. The farmer draws one or more fields on a map.
  2. Patato looks up the field: 25 years of weather, soil type, past crops from USDA satellite crop maps, and how much water the field actually used, measured by satellite. The farmer checks this and fixes anything wrong.
  3. The farmer answers a few questions: is it irrigated, where the water comes from, how reliable the water is, what they grow now, and what matters most to them (saving water, soil health, income, low risk).
  4. Patato shows the current crop plus the 4 best options. Each one shows, in plain words, its water risk in a dry year, income compared with now, its effect on the soil, and practical watch-outs like needing a buyer contract or special equipment.

How it works

  • Can it grow here? A crop suitability engine checks each crop against the field's temperatures, frost dates, rain and soil, and suggests planting and harvest windows.
  • How likely is a dry year? 25 years of growing-season rain at the field are split into dry, normal and wet years. In winter, live snowpack from Boise River snow stations shifts those odds: low snow makes a dry year more likely.
  • Water: for each crop and year type, we compare the water the crop needs (measured locally, and on the farmer's own field for their current crop) with the water they will have. When water is short, yield drops using the FAO-33 standard yield-response formula.
  • Income: yield times price minus cost, from USDA and university budgets. We show it only as a comparison with the current crop, because exact profit depends on each farmer's own costs.
  • Ranking: the farmer's own priorities weight water risk, income and soil health.

Benefits

Farmers see, before planting, which crops will still work if the water runs short, using the same kind of data water managers use. It's honest about uncertainty: every assumption and data source is listed in the app.

Tools

Vue 3, Vite and Leaflet (map) for the website; Python and FastAPI for the backend; deployed on Vercel. Code: https://github.com/santiago28b/crop-rotation

Scope

Built and tuned for southwest Idaho (Treasure Valley). The weather and satellite parts work anywhere; other regions need their own crop costs and water rules.

NASA data

  • NASA POWER (daily agroclimatology, 2001–2025): the base of the whole app. For each field we pull 25 years of daily temperature, rain, humidity, wind, sunlight and soil wetness. We use it to find frost dates and safe planting windows, count hot days, measure crop water demand, and split past years into dry, normal and wet so we know how often a dry year happens.
  • OpenET (a NASA-led project, built mainly on NASA/USGS Landsat satellite data): satellite-measured water use for the farmer's own field, 2023–2025. We use it to tell whether the field looks irrigated, and as the real water need for the crop they grow now.
  • Landsat (through USDA's Cropland Data Layer): the USDA crop map is made from Landsat and other satellite imagery. We use it to find what was planted on the field in past years, which drives rotation advice.

NASA data also inspired the main idea: satellites can see water use and weather risk over decades, which a single farmer can't track by hand.

Space agency partner and other data

We did not use space agency partner data. Other data and tools:

Source

What we used it for

NRCS SNOTEL (USDA)

Live snowpack at 4 Boise River snow stations vs. the 30-year median, to shift the odds of a dry year

USDA Cropland Data Layer (CropScape)

Past crops on the field

USDA NRCS SSURGO soil survey

Soil type, pH and drainage (US)

ISRIC SoilGrids

Backup soil data outside the US survey

USDA NASS QuickStats

Idaho crop yields and prices, 2020–2025 averages

USBR AgriMet, Parma, Idaho station

Measured seasonal water use for each crop

University of Idaho and Oregon State University crop budgets

Cost per acre to grow each crop

FAO EcoCrop and FAO-33

Crop growing ranges, and how yield drops when water is short

FCC Census Area API

The field's state and county

OpenStreetMap and Leaflet

The map

All sources are listed in the app and in the repo's docs/data-sources.md.

Use of artificial intelligence

We used AI tools throughout the project, and the team reviewed, tested and decided on everything:

  • Claude (Anthropic) and Claude Code: helped write a large part of the code (Python backend, scoring logic, data connectors, tests, and parts of the Vue website), plus documentation and this submission text. It also helped research which datasets to use.
  • Gemini (Google): used for early brainstorming of the project idea. The transcript is in the repo at docs/gemini-ideation-transcript.md.
  • AI-assisted data work: an AI agent helped look up and fill in the sourced crop numbers in data/crops.csv. Every number is linked to its source in docs/data-sources.md, and we checked them.
  • The app itself does not use AI to make recommendations. The ranking comes from the data and formulas described above.
  • The app's small animations (the satellite and the potato) were drawn as code (SVG) with AI help. They contain no NASA logos or branding. No AI-generated photos, video or audio.

Our own work: the idea and the farmer interview, choosing what matters to farmers (water risk), product decisions, the design, testing, and deployment.
